title: Two Festivals of Light, Compared Fairly
objective: Read two approved source cards on festivals of light, record what each source says the light stands for, and write one comparison sentence that names both festivals and ranks neither.

blocks.text: GROW · Humanities · Week 6. RE and World Views. Two Festivals of Light, Compared Fairly.
Objective: read two approved source cards on festivals of light, record what each source says the light stands for, and write one comparison sentence that names both festivals and ranks neither.
Success evidence: a comparison grid filled from both cards, and one sentence that names both festivals with no ranking word in it.
Everything you write comes from the source cards. You report what a source says. Nobody is asked what they believe, what they celebrate, or what happens at home.
40 minutes. Offline.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Both source cards face down on each desk before pupils sit. Card A and Card B together, one pair each.
stages.data-ta2: If a pupil starts talking about their own festival or home, thank them and point at the card. Say: today we report only what the card says.

blocks.text: You already hold one lamp
In week 4 you read the approved Hanukkah source.
One more light was added on each of the eight nights.
Today you meet a second festival of light.
It is Diwali, and the source card calls its lamp a diya.
Retrieve the week 4 lamp before the new card is turned over. A pupil holding one festival already can compare; a pupil holding none can only copy.
Comparing means putting two things side by side, not picking a winner.
You need both source cards, the comparison grid and a pen.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Read both example sentences aloud. Do not say yet which one fails.

blocks.text: Two sentences from the same two cards
Here are two sentences written from today's cards.
Sentence one says Diwali uses lots of lamps, but Hanukkah is better.
Sentence two says both festivals light lamps, and each source gives its own reason.
Sentence one adds a judgement that neither card made.
Sentence two reports only what is printed on the cards.

items: 1 · read one card at a time.
2 · record what that card actually says.
3 · ask both cards the same question.
4 · write one sentence that names both.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Model Card A only. Leave Card B for the group or they will copy your wording.

blocks.text: Building one comparison from the cards
I take Card A first, the Diwali card.
The card says rows of small clay lamps are lit.
It says those lamps are called diyas, and that the light stands for good over evil.
I write those three things in the Card A column.
I add nothing I half remember from somewhere else.

blocks.caption: The grid is filled before the sentence is written
blocks.title: From source card to comparison
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: read a card, record what it says, line both cards up on one question, then write the sentence

blocks.text: Now the step people skip: I ask both cards the same question.
My question is what the light stands for.
If I ask Card A about meaning and Card B about dates, nothing lines up.
Say the same-question rule aloud twice. Mismatched questions are the usual reason a full grid still produces no comparison.
So each row of the grid holds one question only.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Every table sorts before anyone speaks. Hold the discussion until all six cards are placed.

blocks.text: Sort the cards, then match them
You have six statement cards, all taken from the two sources.
Sort them into two groups: Card A statements and Card B statements.
Then match each statement to the question it answers.
The three questions are what is lit, when it is lit, and what it stands for.
One statement is true of both festivals. Put that one in the middle.
Hold up the card you argued about most.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Both cards face up, side by side. If a pupil offers a detail that is not on a card, ask them to point to the line that says it.

blocks.text: Reporting a difference without ranking it
Card B says one more light is added each night.
Card A says many lamps are lit on the same night.
That is a real difference and you may write it.
The trap is the next word you reach for.

blocks.caption: Same two cards, and only one version can be checked against them
blocks.title: Reporting against ranking
blocks.alt: Two boxes side by side: a reported difference names both sources, a ranked one adds a judgement the cards do not carry

blocks.text: Better, worse, only and proper all rank a festival.
Both, each and while report it instead.
So write that both festivals light lamps, while each gives its own reason.
One more rule: write according to Card A, and never write everyone thinks.
One date can also hold more than one meaning.
Card A says Sikhs mark a different event at the same time.
You report both meanings, and you choose between neither.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Give one minute for the draft, then pair by table, not by choice. Call each swap aloud.

blocks.text: Hunt the ranking word
First write one draft comparison sentence on scrap paper.
Build it from the statement cards you sorted a moment ago.
Then work in twos. Swap drafts and read your partner's sentence.
Underline any word that puts one festival above the other.
Name the word you found. Do not say the sentence is wrong.
Your partner swaps that word for both, each or while.
Then swap back and read your own draft again.
If there is no ranking word, check that both festivals are named.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe the pupil's exact words. Do not repair a ranking word for them; underline it and hand it back.
stages.data-ta2: A pupil who asks which festival is right is told that the cards do not answer that, and is pointed back to the grid.

blocks.text: Fill the grid, then write the sentence
Work on your own now. Both cards stay on your desk.
The grid has three rows: what is lit, when, and what it stands for.
Every box reports one card in your own words.
Leave a box empty if the card does not say.
An empty box is honest, and a guessed box is not.
Then write your comparison sentence under the grid.
Use the draft your partner checked, or write a stronger one.
Name both festivals and use both, each or while.
Then underline the part of your sentence that came from Card B.

items: Supported · fill one row for both cards, then write one sentence naming both.
Standard · fill all three rows and write one comparison sentence with no ranking word.
Stretch · as Standard, and add a second sentence on a difference the cards report.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: The named adult reads the sentence back word for word, then asks the ranking question only.

blocks.text: Read your sentence to one adult
Read your comparison sentence to the adult at your table.
They read it back exactly as you wrote it.
Then they ask one question: does this rank either festival?
If it does, change that one word and read it again.
Then choose what happens next: keep the grid, add a third source card, or rewrite the sentence.
Write your choice and today's date on the sheet before you leave.

print.intro: Fill the grid from the two source cards only, and leave a box empty rather than guessing what a card does not say.
focusRows: Three rows filled for both cards, from the source cards only
One comparison sentence that names both festivals
No word that puts one festival above the other
tiers: Fill one row for both cards and write one sentence that names both festivals.
Fill all three rows and write one comparison sentence with no ranking word in it.
As Standard, and add a second sentence reporting a difference that the cards state.
checks: Both columns are filled from the approved source cards, not from memory.
Each row asks the same question of both festivals.
The comparison sentence names both festivals and reports what each source says.
No ranking word appears, and boxes the cards do not answer are left empty.
